title: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad
summary: How the House of Wisdom in Baghdad gathered books and scholars from many lands, translated them into Arabic, and produced new ideas in math, science, and astronomy that later spread across the world.
poll: Sharing knowledge between countries makes the whole world smarter.

versions.title: A House Full of Books
versions.text:
Long ago, there was a big city. It was Baghdad. It was by a wide river. The sun was hot. Folks came there to learn.

The city had a big library. Its name was the House of Wisdom. It had lots of books.

Smart men worked there. Each was a scholar. They got old books from far lands. They read the books. Then they wrote them in Arabic. That is to translate. It was a big job. Now more folks could read them.

Paper helped a lot. It was cheap. So it was not hard to make books.

They had new thoughts, too. One man wrote a math book. It gave us a new word. The word is "algebra." He helped spread our numbers, too.

Some of them looked at the stars. They made maps of the sky.

Then, in 1258, an army took the city. It was a sad time. Lots of books were lost. But the ideas did not die. They had gone far and wide. We still use them now.

versions.title: The House of Wisdom: Baghdad's Golden Age of Learning
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, Baghdad was one of the largest and wealthiest cities on Earth. Founded in 762 as the capital of the Abbasid caliphs, it stood beside the Tigris River, and merchants, travelers, and students arrived there from distant lands.

Several Abbasid rulers, especially the caliph al-Ma'mun, valued learning and generously supported scholars. With their patronage, a magnificent library and center of study developed, which became known as the House of Wisdom.

Scholars there collected ancient manuscripts from Greece, Persia, and India and carefully translated them into Arabic. Translators such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq became famous for their accuracy. By working together, scholars from many backgrounds helped preserve knowledge that might otherwise have been lost.

Paper made this work considerably easier. Craftspeople in Baghdad learned to manufacture paper, which was far less expensive than the animal skins used previously, so books became easier to reproduce and distribute.

The scholars did more than repeat old ideas; they also made original discoveries. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote a book whose title gave us the word "algebra," and his own name gave us the word "algorithm," a set of steps for solving a problem. His work also helped spread the numbers we use today. Meanwhile, three brothers known as the Banu Musa designed ingenious machines, including fountains that operated automatically.

Medicine flourished as well. Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated dozens of works by the ancient Greek physician Galen, and these texts were used to train doctors for centuries. Al-Ma'mun reportedly even sent messengers to distant lands to collect valuable manuscripts for translation.

Astronomers built an observatory to study the stars and planets, produced detailed charts of the sky, and even calculated the size of the Earth.

In 1258, a Mongol army captured Baghdad, and countless books were destroyed. However, the ideas had already traveled widely. Later, they were translated into Latin in Europe, where they helped spark new learning. That legacy continues whenever we solve an equation today.

versions.title: The House of Wisdom: Baghdad's Golden Age of Learning
versions.text:
More than a thousand years in the past, Baghdad ranked among the largest and most prosperous cities anywhere on Earth. Founded in 762 as the capital of the Abbasid caliphate, the city rose beside the banks of the Tigris River, steadily attracting merchants, travelers, and aspiring students from remarkably distant regions throughout the known world.

Several successive Abbasid rulers, most notably the caliph al-Ma'mun, placed considerable value upon intellectual pursuits and generously extended their patronage to visiting scholars. Under this sustained royal patronage, an extraordinary library and center of learning gradually developed within the city, one that eventually became known throughout history as the House of Wisdom.

Scholars gathered there acquired ancient manuscripts originating from Greece, Persia, and India, meticulously translating them into Arabic and thereby transforming the city into an extraordinary meeting point for diverse intellectual traditions from across the known world. Translators such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq achieved considerable renown for their extraordinary accuracy and linguistic precision, and through sustained collaboration, scholars drawn from remarkably diverse cultural backgrounds helped preserve knowledge that might otherwise have vanished entirely from the historical record.

The widespread availability of paper rendered this ambitious undertaking considerably more feasible. Craftspeople resident in Baghdad had mastered the manufacture of paper, a material far less costly than the animal skins previously employed for writing, and consequently books became markedly easier both to reproduce in quantity and to distribute widely.

These scholars, moreover, did far more than merely repeat preexisting ideas; they made genuinely original contributions of lasting significance. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi composed an influential treatise whose very title ultimately gave rise to the modern word "algebra," while his own personal name similarly gave rise to the word "algorithm," denoting a systematic sequence of steps employed to solve a given problem. His work additionally helped popularize the numerals still used throughout the world today. Meanwhile, three brothers collectively known as the Banu Musa designed remarkably ingenious mechanical devices, including fountains capable of operating entirely automatically, and meticulously described them within their celebrated Book of Ingenious Devices.

Medicine flourished equally within this scholarly environment: Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated dozens of treatises authored by the ancient Greek physician Galen, and these translated texts subsequently educated practicing physicians across both the Islamic world and Europe for many centuries thereafter. According to surviving historical accounts, al-Ma'mun even dispatched dedicated messengers to distant territories specifically in order to acquire valuable manuscripts suitable for translation, a practice demonstrating precisely how highly the Abbasid court prized scientific and philosophical literature.

Astronomers associated with the institution constructed a dedicated observatory specifically to study the stars and planets, produced remarkably detailed celestial charts, and even calculated the Earth's circumference with genuinely impressive precision for their era.

In 1258, an invading Mongol army captured Baghdad, and countless irreplaceable volumes were tragically destroyed in the resulting devastation. Nevertheless, the underlying ideas had already traveled widely beyond the city's walls, and they were subsequently translated into Latin throughout Europe, where they helped stimulate considerable new scholarship. That enduring intellectual legacy persists to this day whenever any student anywhere solves a mathematical equation.

versions.title: The House of Wisdom: Baghdad's Golden Age of Learning
versions.text:
More than a thousand years in the past, Baghdad ranked among the largest, wealthiest, and most intellectually vibrant cities anywhere on the Earth. Founded in 762 as the political capital of the Abbasid caliphate, the city rose beside the banks of the Tigris River, steadily attracting merchants, travelers, and aspiring students from remarkably distant regions throughout the entire known world of its era.

Several successive Abbasid rulers, most notably the caliph al-Ma'mun, placed considerable and sustained value upon intellectual pursuits of every kind and generously extended their royal patronage to visiting scholars from diverse backgrounds. Under this sustained patronage, an extraordinary library and center of advanced learning gradually developed within the city itself, one that eventually became known throughout subsequent history as the House of Wisdom.

Scholars gathered there systematically acquired ancient manuscripts originating from Greece, Persia, and India, meticulously translating them into Arabic and thereby transforming the city into an extraordinary meeting point for disparate intellectual traditions converging from across the known world. Translators such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq achieved considerable and lasting renown for their extraordinary linguistic accuracy and precision, and through sustained, collaborative effort, scholars drawn from remarkably diverse cultural and religious backgrounds collectively helped preserve knowledge that might otherwise have vanished entirely from the historical record during subsequent centuries of upheaval.

The widespread availability of paper rendered this ambitious intellectual undertaking considerably more logistically feasible. Craftspeople resident in Baghdad had thoroughly mastered the manufacture of paper, a material far less costly to produce than the animal skins previously employed for writing purposes, and consequently books became markedly easier both to reproduce in substantial quantity and to subsequently distribute across wide geographic areas.

These accomplished scholars, moreover, did considerably more than merely repeat preexisting ideas inherited from earlier civilizations; they made genuinely original and lasting contributions of their own. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi composed an immensely influential treatise whose very title ultimately gave rise to the modern English word "algebra," while his own personal name similarly gave rise to the word "algorithm," denoting a systematic sequence of precise steps employed to solve a given mathematical problem. His pioneering work additionally helped popularize the numeral system still used throughout the world today. Meanwhile, three ingenious brothers collectively known as the Banu Musa designed remarkably sophisticated mechanical devices, including ornamental fountains capable of operating entirely automatically without human intervention, and meticulously documented their designs within their celebrated Book of Ingenious Devices.

Medicine flourished with equal vigor within this rich scholarly environment: Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated dozens of medical treatises originally authored by the ancient Greek physician Galen, and these carefully translated texts subsequently educated practicing physicians across both the Islamic world and medieval Europe for many centuries thereafter. According to surviving historical accounts, al-Ma'mun even dispatched dedicated messengers to distant and sometimes hostile territories specifically in order to acquire valuable manuscripts suitable for subsequent translation, a documented practice demonstrating precisely how highly the Abbasid court prized scientific and philosophical literature of every origin.

Astronomers closely associated with the institution constructed a dedicated observatory specifically intended to study the movements of the stars and planets, produced remarkably detailed celestial charts of enduring scientific value, and even calculated the Earth's circumference with genuinely impressive precision for an era lacking modern instrumentation.

In 1258, an invading Mongol army captured the city of Baghdad outright, and countless irreplaceable volumes of accumulated scholarship were tragically destroyed amid the resulting devastation and chaos. Nevertheless, the underlying ideas themselves had already traveled widely beyond the city's original walls long before this catastrophe, and they were subsequently translated into Latin throughout medieval Europe, where they helped stimulate considerable new scholarship and intellectual inquiry. That enduring intellectual legacy persists vividly to this day, manifesting itself whenever any student anywhere in the world solves a mathematical equation.

questions.stem: Why did translating books into Arabic matter so much?
options: It let people read ideas from many lands in one language.
It made every one of the books much shorter.
It kept the books secret from most people.
It replaced all of the old math books in the city.
questions.why: Arabic was widely read, so translating books brought knowledge from Greece, Persia, and India together for many readers.

wrong.B: Translation does not make books shorter.
wrong.C: The goal was to share the books, not hide them.
wrong.D: Translations added to math knowledge; they did not replace it.

questions.stem: How were the scholars different from people who only copy books?
options: They never read old books.
They wrote only in Greek.
They added new discoveries, like algebra.
They worked alone and never shared.
questions.why: The article says the scholars did more than copy old ideas; they made discoveries, such as al-Khwarizmi's algebra.

wrong.A: They read and translated many old books.
wrong.D: They worked together and shared ideas.

questions.stem: What can readers infer from the fact that scholars tried to measure the size of the Earth?
options: They knew a great deal of math and astronomy.
They thought the Earth was very small.
They did not believe in the stars.
They wanted to build a wall around the city.
questions.why: Measuring the Earth requires careful math and observation of the sky, which shows their skill in both.

wrong.B: The article does not say what size they expected.
wrong.D: Measuring the Earth has nothing to do with walls.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article by saying we still use these ideas today?
options: To show that the House of Wisdom still matters
To argue that Baghdad was never attacked
To explain how to translate a book
To list every scholar's name
questions.why: By connecting the past to today, the author shows the lasting importance of the House of Wisdom.

wrong.B: The article says Baghdad was attacked in 1258.
wrong.C: The ending does not give translating steps.
wrong.D: The ending does not list names.

MID.prompt: Explain how paper and translation together helped knowledge spread from Baghdad to the rest of the world. Use details from the article.
checklist: I used at least two key words such as manuscript, knowledge, or caliph.
MID.modelAnswer: Paper helped because people in Baghdad learned to make it, and it was much cheaper than the animal skins used before, so books were easier to copy and share. Translation also helped because scholars took manuscripts from Greece, Persia, and India and turned them into Arabic, bringing knowledge from many cultures into one place. Together, cheap paper and careful translation let the caliph's scholars spread this knowledge to many more people than before.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The House of Wisdom was mainly a place for storing gold.

wrong.A: The House of Wisdom was a library and center of study.
wrong.C: The caliphs supported translation, especially al-Ma'mun.
wrong.D: The ideas had already spread and continued to influence learning.

Astronomy and observatory

questions.stem: Why did paper make the House of Wisdom's work more effective?

Paper cost far less than animal skins, so books spread more easily.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the report that al-Ma'mun sent messengers to acquire manuscripts?

HIGH.prompt: The House of Wisdom brought together scholars and books from many cultures. Explain why this collaboration produced so many discoveries, using at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained why working together led to discoveries.
I used at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
I used academic words such as preserve, legacy, or algorithm.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The House of Wisdom brought scholars from many cultures together, which helped preserve old knowledge and also create new discoveries. First, scholars translated ancient manuscripts from Greece, Persia, and India into Arabic, which let ideas from different civilizations combine in one place. Second, al-Khwarizmi used this shared foundation of mathematics to write a book that gave us the word algebra, and his name is also the origin of the word algorithm. Third, other scholars studied astronomy and tried to measure the size of the Earth, building on knowledge gathered from many lands. Even though an invading army destroyed many books in 1258, the legacy of this collaboration survived and was later translated again in Europe.
